clue.text: Absorb abstract

blocks.note: first meaning: to take in and assimilate, as food or information
second meaning: a short summary of a longer text

explanation.walkthrough: Both words look like a pair of verbs, but the second is a noun: a summary of a paper.
explanation.definitionFit: One word is a verb for taking in food or ideas and a noun for a condensed summary of writing.

clue.text: Bird with modern date reflected on old one with bumpkin

indicators.note: a reflection in a mirror shows things the wrong way round, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: AD, anno Domini, marks a date in the modern era
BC marks an old date, before Christ
a hick is an unsophisticated country person

explanation.surface: A bird ringed with a modern date tag sits on an ancient one beside a country yokel.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' puts the reversed modern date above the old one: DA + BC + HICK.
explanation.definitionFit: The dabchick is the little grebe, a small diving waterbird of ponds and lakes.

clue.text: Look into what happens in casinos at twilight

indicators.note: one word going into another means it is placed inside it

blocks.note: gambling is what goes on in a casino
lo is an old exclamation meaning look

explanation.surface: An invitation to peek into a casino as evening falls.
explanation.definitionFit: Gloaming is a chiefly Scottish and poetic word for dusk, the dim light after sunset.

clue.text: Cooks in house of ill repute

blocks.note: first meaning: simmers slowly in liquid
second meaning: an archaic word for a brothel

explanation.surface: Kitchen work going on inside a brothel.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is old-fashioned: 'the stews' were the brothels of medieval London.
explanation.definitionFit: The plural noun once meant a brothel or the district of brothels; the verb means slow simmering.

clue.text: Outer layer of letter I fire shells at

blocks.note: Ep. is the abbreviation for epistle, a letter, in Bible references
taken as written
to blast a target is to bombard it

explanation.surface: Someone describing their bombardment of the outer layer of a letter.
explanation.walkthrough: Ep. as short for epistle is the hardest piece; 'fire shells at' is one unit meaning blast.
explanation.definitionFit: In embryology the epiblast is the outermost layer of cells in the early embryo, which becomes the ectoderm.

clue.text: Worker on trial is in concert in part of church

indicators.note: placing something in a concert puts it inside the word for that event

blocks.note: a test is a trial
the worker ant is the crossword's stock worker
taken as written
a prom is a promenade concert

explanation.surface: A labourer facing trial during a concert in a church.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' puts the worker below the trial. A prom is a promenade concert, as in the BBC Proms.
explanation.definitionFit: Protestantism is the branch of Western Christianity that split from Rome at the Reformation.

clue.text: Charge a toll at the dwindling river

blocks.note: a bill is a charge for goods or services
taken as written
a bell's toll is its bong

explanation.surface: Someone collecting a fee at a shrinking river crossing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'toll' looks like a fee alongside 'Charge', but here it is the sound of a bell.
explanation.definitionFit: A billabong is an Australian backwater or cut-off pool left when a river channel stops flowing.

clue.text: A blow grips university, falling between academic years

indicators.note: to grip something is to hold it tightly within

blocks.note: a + gust, a blow of wind
U is the abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: A blow strikes a university during the summer gap between academic years.
explanation.walkthrough: The university letter goes in after the A, not at the start of the blow.
explanation.definitionFit: The month comes during the long summer vacation, after one school year ends and before the next starts.

clue.text: Label lacking head and heart

indicators.note: having no head means the first letter is cut away

blocks.note: a sticker is an adhesive label

explanation.surface: A label missing both its head and its heart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head and heart' reads as a pair, but only 'head' belongs to the wordplay; 'heart' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Ticker is informal slang for the heart, from its regular beating like a clock.

clue.text: The common man, being skint, changes sides

indicators.note: switching sides swaps right for left, so one letter is exchanged for its opposite

blocks.note: skint is British slang for having no money

explanation.surface: An ordinary man, out of money, switches political allegiance.
explanation.walkthrough: R (right) becomes L (left) in BROKE. Skint is British slang for penniless.
explanation.definitionFit: Bloke is British slang for an ordinary man, a regular guy or chap.

clue.text: Work record brought into smart but specious argument

indicators.note: bringing something into another word places it inside

blocks.note: op is short for opus, a work
a log is a written record
chic means stylish or smart

explanation.surface: A work record tucked into a clever but misleading case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'smart but specious' reads as one description of the argument, but 'smart' belongs to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Chop-logic is overly subtle, sophistical reasoning that seems clever but is unsound.

clue.text: On the way up, stitch up playground feature

blocks.note: climbing means ascending
to stitch someone up is to frame them for a crime

explanation.surface: Someone rising in the world while betraying a colleague at the playground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stitch up' is British slang for falsely incriminating someone.
explanation.definitionFit: A climbing frame is a structure of bars children clamber over in a park, a jungle gym.

clue.text: Headhunter's current employment in part of England

blocks.note: the head of the hunter is its opening letter; the apostrophe-s just joins it on
amps measure electric current
hire is employment for payment

explanation.surface: A recruiter's present job is based somewhere in England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Headhunter' looks like one word for a recruiter, but it splits into 'Head' and 'hunter'.
explanation.definitionFit: Hampshire is a county on the south coast of England, home to Southampton and Winchester.

clue.text: The compiler is to report to the gangway

indicators.note: a report is something heard, so the words are to be taken by their sound

blocks.note: the compiler is I, and 'I am to' becomes I will, shortened

explanation.surface: The setter is due to present themselves at a ship's gangway.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter calls themselves 'the compiler', which stands for I.
explanation.definitionFit: An aisle is a passage between rows of seats, as a gangway is in a theatre or plane.

clue.text: Feeling bad about being unimpressed, initially, by the widow's mite, say

indicators.note: initially means taking the first letter of each word
one word lying about another surrounds it

blocks.note: contrition is remorse for having done wrong
the opening letters of these two words

explanation.surface: Someone feels guilty about being unmoved by a poor widow's offering.
explanation.walkthrough: The widow's mite is from the Gospels: a poor widow gave two tiny coins, all she had, to the temple.
explanation.definitionFit: The widow's two small coins were a donation, the classic example of a small gift worth more than large ones.

clue.text: A contralto not keeping time, perhaps, in gummy passage?

indicators.note: not keeping something means it is dropped from the letters
perhaps suggests the letters might be arranged some other way

blocks.note: taken as written
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A singer losing the beat in some sticky passage of music.
explanation.walkthrough: One T is removed from A CONTRALTO and the rest rearranged. The question mark flags the playful definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The canal inside a tooth's root lies below the gum, so it is a passage in the gums, jokingly.

clue.text: Boy and girl rising for a piece of music

indicators.note: in a down clue rising means read upwards, so the letters go backwards

blocks.note: a son is a boy
Anita is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A boy and a girl stand up to perform a piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A sonatina is a short, simple sonata, a small instrumental composition.

clue.text: Denmark, a hyperactive place with a platform for free speech

definitions.text: place with a platform for free speech

indicators.note: being active means busy and moving about, so the letters stir

blocks.note: DK is the international vehicle code for Denmark
taken as written
the first five letters, taken as written; the rest of the word is the signal

explanation.surface: Denmark is described as a manic country with a soapbox for open speech.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hyperactive' must be split: the first part is fodder and 'active' is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: London's Hyde Park contains Speakers' Corner, where anyone may stand and address the public.

clue.text: Bloom given praise before 12

blocks.note: the hours before noon
glory is praise, as in giving glory to God

explanation.surface: A flower receives compliments before noon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'praise before 12' reads as one phrase, but the time comes first in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The morning glory is a climbing plant with trumpet-shaped flowers that open in the early part of the day.

clue.text: Certain to secure second victory, standing against...

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it firmly enclosed
in a down clue standing up means reading from the bottom, so backwards

blocks.note: sure means certain
S is the abbreviation for second
V for victory

explanation.surface: Someone sure of winning a second time takes a stand in opposition.
explanation.walkthrough: S goes inside SURE, V is added, then the whole is turned up: SUSREV upside down. The dots lead into the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Versus is Latin for turned toward, used to mean against, as in a court case or match.

clue.text: ... last of Hague's Tories, I lost badly, needing two speakers

definitions.note: adjective phrase for sound played through two channels

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter
something lost is gone, so that letter is dropped
doing badly suggests things are in disarray, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: only the final letter of this name
taken as written
the letter removed

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue, William Hague's Conservatives lost badly and needed two spokesmen.
explanation.walkthrough: William Hague led the Tories to a heavy 2001 election defeat. I is removed from TORIES and E added before shuffling.
explanation.definitionFit: Stereophonic sound uses two channels played through a pair of loudspeakers, left and right.

clue.text: Weapon carried by livestock?

indicators.note: something carried by a word is held within its letters

blocks.note: the middle stretch of this word

explanation.surface: A question about whether farm animals bear arms.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that cattle bearing weapons is absurd.
explanation.definitionFit: An estoc is a long, stiff medieval thrusting sword designed to pierce armour.

clue.text: Markets dramatist, getting a reasonable cut

blocks.note: fairs are markets
David Hare is an English playwright

explanation.surface: A playwright selling at markets earns a decent percentage.
explanation.definitionFit: A fair share is an equitable portion, a just slice of profits or spoils.

clue.text: Smashed the oven

blocks.note: first meaning: past tense of stave in, to break inwards
second meaning: a kitchen appliance for cooking

explanation.surface: Someone broke the oven.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smashed the oven' reads as one action; the first word is the past tense of stave, as in staved or stove in a boat.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun is a cooking appliance like a range; the verb form is the past of stave, to break inwards.

clue.text: Bullying the astronaut is out of order

indicators.note: out of order means the parts are not in their usual sequence

blocks.note: Neil Armstrong, the first person on the Moon

explanation.surface: Accusing a spaceman of bullying, which is unacceptable behaviour.
explanation.walkthrough: The surname's two halves swap places. 'Out of order' in the surface means unacceptable.
explanation.definitionFit: Strong-arm tactics use force or threats to coerce someone, which is intimidation.

clue.text: Sounding bored with remote access?

blocks.note: surface reading: someone sounding weary
setter's reading: a board, punned by sound, for contacting the dead at a distance

explanation.walkthrough: 'bored' plays on board, and 'remote access' is reaching spirits on the other side. The name also joins French and German words for yes.
explanation.definitionFit: The talking board used at seances lets spirits supposedly spell out messages from the beyond.

clue.text: Start to shrivel and decay, as passion may

definitions.note: a clause standing for the verb

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: only the opening letter
to moulder is to rot slowly

explanation.surface: Something begins to wither and rot, the way a love affair might.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole clause: passion may burn slowly without flame.
explanation.definitionFit: Feelings that smoulder burn inwardly, suppressed, like a fire glowing without flames.

clue.text: Notice cinematic litigant's return

indicators.note: a return goes back the way it came, so the name runs backwards

blocks.note: Kramer vs Kramer is a 1979 film about a custody battle

explanation.surface: Pay attention to a film character's comeback in court.
explanation.definitionFit: To remark is to observe or take note of something, as a noun also a comment.
